title: Sell Mineral Rights in Waynesburg, PA
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Waynesburg, PA
metaDescription: Own mineral rights in Waynesburg, the Greene County seat? We buy Marcellus interests directly, explain split-estate issues honestly, and pay cash.
heroLead: Waynesburg families have lived with two different underground industries for a long time, coal that's been mined for generations and gas that showed up more recently, and untangling which rights belong to which can take real work.
intro: Waynesburg is the Greene County seat, sitting in what many consider the deepest, wettest part of the entire Marcellus play in Pennsylvania. Greene County's rock has consistently drawn some of the most aggressive operator interest in the Commonwealth, with CNX and EQT both maintaining substantial positions here, and the county's impact fee revenue under Act 13 reflects just how much unconventional development has concentrated in this corner of the state.

That intensity comes with a wrinkle unique to Greene County: extensive longwall coal mining runs underneath a lot of the same land where Marcellus gas is being produced, creating a split-estate situation where coal rights, gas rights, and surface rights can all belong to different owners on the very same tract.

sections.heading: Split Estates Between Coal and Gas
paragraphs: If your family owns gas rights near Waynesburg, it's worth confirming whether coal rights on the same land belong to a mining company, since longwall mining can affect surface conditions and occasionally complicates well spacing or unit boundaries. This doesn't diminish your gas rights, but understanding the full picture matters when evaluating your interest.

We see this constantly in Greene County specifically. It's less common in counties without a heavy underground coal mining history, which is part of why Waynesburg-area deeds sometimes need more careful reading than a straightforward farm tract elsewhere in the state.

sections.heading: Why This Is Some of the Most Active Ground in the State
paragraphs: Greene County's position deep in the wet-gas window has kept it among the busiest drilling counties in Pennsylvania for over a decade, and Waynesburg-area units frequently show strong, sustained production numbers. That gives us real data to work from when building an offer rather than relying on speculation.

sections.heading: Deductions, the Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act, and Act 13
paragraphs: Pennsylvania's Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act sets a one-eighth floor on gross value, but post-production deductions permitted under many Greene County leases, upheld broadly by Kilmer v. Elexco, can still shrink your net check well below what the reported gas price would suggest. Act 13 impact fees, meanwhile, fund county and township infrastructure directly from the operator and have no bearing on your personal royalty statement, even though Greene County collects some of the largest impact fee distributions in the state.

faqs.question: How do I know if coal mining under my land affects my gas rights?
faqs.answer: Check your deed for a separate coal reservation, and we can help cross-reference that against known longwall mining areas. Coal and gas ownership are typically independent of each other even on the same tract.

faqs.question: Why is Greene County considered such an active drilling area?
faqs.answer: The rock here sits deep in the wet-gas Marcellus window, which has consistently drawn strong operator interest from companies like CNX and EQT for well over a decade.

faqs.question: My royalty check seems small relative to the gas price I see reported. Why?
faqs.answer: Post-production deductions for gathering, compression, and transportation are the most common reason, particularly on older leases. We review your specific lease language to explain the gap.

faqs.question: Does Greene County's large impact fee revenue affect my royalty?
faqs.answer: No. Act 13 impact fees are paid by operators to county and township government and are entirely separate from the royalty calculation on your personal division order.
